input.question: Why are some Roman names anglicized to drop their us at the end (Hadrianus to Hadrian) while others were not? Why do we have an Emperor Marcus and not an Emperor Tit or August?
input.ground_truth: Followup question, my last name is August and I can trace myself back to Lithuania as "Augustinavicious" (anglicized). Would there be any connections between Augustus and Augustinavicious? My personal guess is "august" being a loanword, but I'm amazed it made it's way to Lithuania.

Question: Why are some Roman names anglicized to drop their us at the end (Hadrianus to Hadrian) while others were not? Why do we have an Emperor Marcus and not an Emperor Tit or August?

response.prediction:
Okay, let’s imagine you have a bunch of friends with long names, like “Lucius” or “Marcus.” Sometimes, when people from far away move to a new place (like the Romans moving to England), they start using shorter, easier names that sound good in the new language. So, “Hadrianus” becomes “Hadrian” because it’s easier to say.

Some names, like “Marcus,” already sound nice and simple, so people keep them just the way they are. But other names, like “Titus,” sometimes get shortened or changed a little to fit in better, but we still use “Titus” or “Tiberius” instead of just “Tit” or “Tib,” because those short versions don’t sound right or important.

Also, emperors and important people usually keep their full, big names to sound important and special, not just a tiny part of their name. So, we say “Emperor Marcus,” not “Emperor Tit,” because “Marcus” sounds more complete and grand!
